question: How do Docker containers differ from traditional Virtual Machines (VMs) in terms of kernel sharing and resource overhead?

options.text: VMs virtualize hardware and run an entire guest OS kernel.

It allows compiling dependencies (which requires heavy build tools and compilers like gcc) in an ephemeral stage and copying only pure wheels to a minimal slim production image, cutting image size from 1 GB to $< 80$ MB.
If a hacker exploits a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in a root container, they gain root access to the host kernel.
It forces Python to flush standard output immediately to the terminal stdout stream, ensuring logs appear in docker logs and CloudWatch in real time without lag.

explanation: VMs virtualize hardware and run an entire guest OS kernel. Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate processes using Linux namespaces and cgroups, booting in milliseconds with negligible RAM overhead.
